transcript.text: The extractor fan over my hob has stopped working. Lights come on but the fan just hums when I press the speed buttons, doesn't spin. It's a Bosch chimney hood I think. Is that part of my hob?

## Is it part of the hob?

No. A chimney hood is a separate appliance from your hob, even though it sits directly above it. It usually has its own power supply (often a fused spur switch on the wall nearby or a plug in the chimney housing) and its own model number. So the hob itself isn't faulty, and you'll want to look up parts or repairs for the hood specifically.

(The exception is a hob with a built-in downdraft extractor in the cooktop, but since you have a chimney hood on the wall above, that's not your setup.)

## Why it hums but doesn't spin

The lights and controls work and the motor is getting power, so the problem is almost certainly in the motor itself. The usual culprits are:

1. Seized or stiff motor bearings (most common). Years of grease and heat dry out the bearings so the motor can't turn.
2. Failed motor capacitor. This small component gives the motor its "kick" to start. When it fails, the motor hums but won't start turning.
3. Obstruction. Something is jamming the fan wheel (impeller), such as a build-up of grease or a dislodged part.

## What you can check yourself

First, switch off and isolate the power at the fused spur or unplug it, not just at the hood buttons.

1. Remove the grease filters (they normally unclip from underneath) and look up at the fan housing for anything obviously blocking it.
2. Try turning the fan by hand. If you can reach the impeller, give it a gentle spin.
• Stiff, gritty, or won't move: likely seized bearings. Usually this means a replacement motor.
• Spins freely and keeps coasting: the bearings are probably fine, which points to the capacitor.
3. Tip: if it spins freely, you can try (carefully, and only as a test) giving it a nudge with a wooden spoon handle right after switching it on. If it then runs normally, the capacitor is almost certainly the problem. Don't put fingers near it while powered.

## Fixing it

• Find the model number. It's on a rating plate, usually visible once the grease filters are removed. It'll start with something like "DWB…" or "DWK…" for Bosch. You need this to order the right part.
• Capacitor: a cheap part (often under £15) and a fairly simple swap if you're comfortable with basic electrics. Capacitors can hold a charge, so take care.
• Motor: typically £50 to £150 depending on the model. It's a more involved job but still doable for a confident DIYer.
• Warranty: if the hood is less than two years old (or you registered it for an extended warranty), contact Bosch before opening it up.
• If you're not comfortable working inside it, an appliance repair engineer can usually sort this in one visit.

If you can find the model number, I can help you work out which parts it uses.

Thanks. The filters are pretty greasy, I haven't cleaned them in about a year. I haven't looked at the fan and I'm not climbing a ladder to take it apart. I don't know the model number either. Also, there's a slightly warm smell if I leave it humming for a minute or so. Is it ok to keep using it?

## Is it OK to keep using it?

No, stop using the fan until it's fixed. The warm smell is a warning sign. When a motor hums but can't turn, it draws power without moving, and that energy turns into heat. Left like that, the motor windings can overheat, damage the motor further, or in the worst case become a fire risk, especially with greasy filters and grease build-up just below.

What to do for now:

• Don't press the fan buttons. If it hums, switch it off straight away.
• Ideally isolate the power at the fused spur switch on the wall (or unplug it) until it's repaired. That way nobody presses a button by mistake.
• The lights alone are low risk, but if you isolate the hood you'll lose them too. A bit of inconvenience is worth the peace of mind.
• Cook with a window open or use a lid to manage steam and smells in the meantime.

## Things you can do without a ladder

Clean the filters. They unclip from underneath, which you can usually reach standing at the hob. After a year, they're worth cleaning regardless of the fan problem, since built-up grease is a fire risk on its own. Most Bosch metal mesh filters can go in the dishwasher on a hot cycle (on their own, as they can discolour other items), or soak them in hot water with washing-up liquid or a degreaser. Note that this won't fix the hum, which is a motor issue, but it's good to do.

Find the model number. With the filters out, look up inside the hood. The rating plate is usually a sticker on the inside of the canopy. You may be able to see it from floor level with a torch, or snap a photo with your phone held up inside. Look for an E-Nr (e.g. DWB97...) and FD number. Having this makes getting a repair or part quote much easier.

## Getting it fixed

Since you'd rather not take it apart, I'd hand this one to a professional:

• Bosch's own repair service (bookable through the Bosch Home website) or a local independent appliance engineer. Independents are often cheaper.
• Give them the model number and describe the symptoms ("lights work, motor hums but won't spin, warm smell"). That tells an engineer it's likely the motor or capacitor, so they can bring the right part.
• Worth weighing up: a capacitor is a cheap fix, but if it needs a full replacement motor, the parts plus labour can approach the cost of a basic new hood, particularly if yours is more than about 8 to 10 years old. Ask for a quote before agreeing to the work.
